What is the labor participation rate and how does current year stack up?

I am an expert on this subject. Labor Participation, and the Labor Force Participation Rate:

What is the total available workforce? Basically every working age adult between 16 and 65 years of age.

However, every adult is not actually available. Many are not actually part of the workforce. Many are disabled. Some are retired. Some are wealthy and do not work. Some simply refuse to work. You get the idea.

This reduces the pool of the available workforce. The labor participation rate is the percentage of working aged adults who are either working, or are actively looking for work (trying to be in the work force.) People are between jobs all the time. They quit, get fired, get laid off, get pregnant, move between cities, etc... they are considered to still be in the workforce.

Unemployed means you are a working aged adult, you are not currently working, and you are actively looking for work. You are participating in the labor force. Unemployed does not mean every working aged adult who is not actually working, (which is what most people think it means.)

If you are a working aged adult, you are not working, and you are not looking for work, then you are not in the labor force.

Now, in the United States, labor force participation is generally between 60 to 65% of the total working age population. When the economy is slow, and jobs are harder to find, unemployed people give up looking for work, and they leave the labor force. Labor force participation drops. When the economy is growing, and wages are rising, people who were not looking for work will start to look again, and thus they are returning to the labor force. Labor force participation rises.

The rule for being qualified as participating in the labor force is if you have been actively seeking employment at any time in the last six months.

Under Trump, expectations of an improved economy have lead to a slight increase in the participating labor force. The unemployment rate (those actively looking for work) has also gone down because hiring has improved.

During the tech boom of the 1990's, labor force participation actually averaged between 66% and 67%. This fell during the Bush Jr, and Obama years, and only now is showing early signs of growing again. Depending on how you decide to measure it, there are anywhere from 10 to 20 million Americans who would return to the labor force if they thought it was worth looking for work again, at this time.

Here is a graph which depicts what I have described above:

https://tradingeconomics.com/united-states/labor-force-participation-rate

You may notice the lower average participation rate in the 1950's and 1960's, on the right. That is because most women were not in the paid labor force at that time. Women's liberation brought women into the job market in record numbers, increasing the available labor force.

One final note about Labor Force Participation. It is not yet humanly possible to get an exact accurate count of this rate at any time. Instead, the government uses various survey methods to gather statistics, and then estimates the outcomes for the entire population. There are also several private organizations that follow similar data gathering approaches to obtain similar projections. This means that depending upon your data source, the results are usually different, and dated as well. Even so, a cross section of this data from multiple sources does yield a fairly accurate picture as to both the current situation and the general trend of the economy.
